s: Part four.
Validation and retries.
By the end of this part, you'll know the three levels of checking, how to write feedback that actually gets a correction, and when to stop retrying altogether.
Let's start with a picture.
Hand an essay back with "this is wrong, do it again."
What do you get?
The same essay.
Now circle the sentence.
Write "this quote isn't in any of your sources."
And say "replace it or remove it."
What do you get?
A fixed essay.
This part is about two things.
First.
Checking what the model produced, against things the schema can't see.
Second.
When a check fails, sending feedback specific enough that the next attempt is a correction.
Not a second roll of the dice.
Start with checking.
There are three different questions you can ask of a filled-in form.
One.
Is it legible and complete?
Two.
Does it agree with itself?
Three.
Does it agree with the world?
Teams ship bad data because they only ask the first.
In exam terms, these are the three validation tiers.
Tier one is structural.
Enforcement from part three already handles it.
Tier two is internal semantic.
Does the total equal the sum of the line items?
Is every field named in fields_not_found actually null?
Is the date plausible?
Tier three is external semantic.
Is the supplier in your vendor master?
Does the purchase order number match one you issued?
Does the currency match the contract?
So what's the difference?
Tier two catches a record that contradicts itself.
Only tier three catches a coherent extraction of the wrong document.
And both tiers live in your own application code.
Why?
Because only your code knows what the sum should be, and which suppliers exist.
Now retries.
A retry that resends the identical prompt is a bet.
A bet that the model will randomly come out differently.
It's called pure resampling.
If a failure is systematic, caused by the input or the prompt, it fails the same way again.
And you pay again.
The notes have a neat worked example.
Say a verbatim retry succeeds about fifteen percent of the time.
That tells you roughly fifteen percent of your failures were coin flips.
And the other eighty-five percent will fail identically, forever.
So what does a correcting retry look like?
Three steps.
First.
You append the model's own previous attempt to the conversation, as its turn.
Second.
You send the validation failure back as a tool result, with a flag called is_error set to true.
That keeps the exchange in the channel the model already understands from tool use.
Third.
The error text names four things.
The field.
The observed value.
The rule it broke.
And the next action.
Here's an example.
"Finding seven cites source nineteen, which is not in the retrieved set of sources one to fourteen.
Cite a retrieved source that states this claim, or drop finding seven.
Correct only finding seven."
Then you cap the attempts, and send what's left to a person.
Here's another source disagreement.
Lesson sixteen says cap retries at two.
The notes say three.
And the notes are explicit that three is house guidance, not a platform limit.
It's to be moved once your own data shows where improvement flattens.
So don't argue about the number.
The point is bounded retries that feed back the specific validation error.
One rule sits above any cap.
A failure classified as not retryable, such as a refusal or a permission denial, is not retried at all.
Whatever the counter says.
And log the pattern of failures by field, not just the count.
That distribution tells you which prompt or schema change to make next.
And that closes the loop, back to parts one and two.
Two tempting but wrong retry fixes are worth naming.
First.
Exponential backoff.
That means waiting longer between attempts.
It's for rate limits and temporary infrastructure faults.
Not validation failures.
Waiting doesn't change the input or the prompt.
Second.
Switching to a bigger model.
That treats a feedback defect as a capability shortfall.
A stronger model receiving "try again" still learns nothing.
Quick recap before the questions.
Check at three tiers: shape, self-agreement, and the world.
When a check fails, feed back the field, the value, the rule, and the next step, as a tool result with is_error true.
Cap the attempts.
And never retry what isn't retryable.
Right.
Four practice questions.
Question one.
Here's the scenario.
A synthesis subagent emits findings through a forced tool call.
A validator checks that every cited source exists in the retrieved set.
On failure, the coordinator appends the prior attempt, and replies "Validation failed.
Please try again."
Second attempts mostly fail the same way.
And retries are now a large share of spend.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
Return a tool result with is_error true, naming the finding, the bad source, the rule, and the next step.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: raise the retry cap.
Why?
It multiplies spend on a bet the data shows is losing.
Wrong: drop the prior attempt, so each retry "starts clean."
That sounds fair-minded.
Why is it wrong?
It makes the retry a fresh guess, with no knowledge of what went wrong.
That's the identical-prompt pattern again.
Wrong: route to a larger model.
Why?
The message is still generic.
Question two.
This is the cold open story.
Here's the scenario.
An invoice validator tells the model "total_amount does not equal the sum of line_items, fix it."
The pass rate rises from ninety-one to ninety-nine percent.
But auditors find recorded totals that differ from the printed ones.
Often with a discount line missing.
What's the root cause?
Take a second.
The answer.
The feedback never said the printed total is authoritative.
So the model overwrote it with its own sum.
Picture a clerk handed a receipt that says twenty dollars, when the items add up to twenty-five.
Tell them "make these match," and they may just change the receipt to twenty-five.
Tell them "the printed total is correct, find the item you added wrong," and you get the missing coupon.
So what does better feedback say?
Three things.
It states the numbers, and the difference.
It says: if the printed total really is that figure, keep it, and check for a missed discount or credit.
And it says: do not change the total to match your sum.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: a strict rounding tolerance.
Why?
That would produce small differences, not a missing discount line.
Wrong: a missing pattern on the total.
Why?
It's irrelevant.
The numbers are well formed.
Wrong: a low retry cap.
Why?
These records pass validation.
The loop is ending in "success," not running out of attempts.
Hold on to this line.
Say which side of a discrepancy is authoritative, or the retry fixes the check by destroying the evidence.
Question three.
Here's the scenario.
A warranty-claims agent extracts a purchase date.
Validation requires a date.
For about six percent of emails, the loop fails every time, even with specific feedback.
And review shows those emails simply never state a purchase date.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
Make purchase_date nullable, but still required.
Stop retrying on null.
And route those claims to a person.
Here's the picture.
You can ask someone to re-read a letter for the sender's phone number as often as you like.
If it isn't there, they'll keep failing.
Or they'll start making numbers up.
The key line from the course.
Hold on to this line.
Retries correct formatting.
They cannot make absent information appear.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: raise the cap.
Why?
Specific feedback is already in place.
And it can't conjure a missing date.
Wrong: tell the model to estimate from context.
Why?
That's asking it to fabricate.
And a made-up date then passes validation, and corrupts the claim.
Wrong: run three instances and take the majority date.
Why?
Instances that each must produce a date will each invent one.
And a vote can adopt the invention as consensus.
So what is retry for?
Things like a date written with the month first, when the rule asks for year, then month, then day.
Question four.
Here's the scenario.
An accounts payable pipeline has schema enforcement and internal checks.
Totals reconcile.
And the not-found list matches the nulls.
But audits still find records that are fully self-consistent, yet were extracted from a delivery note or a quote, rather than an invoice.
And some name suppliers the company has never used.
Which addition catches this?
Take a second.
The answer.
Check each extraction against your own reference data.
Such as the vendor master, and issued purchase orders.
Here's the picture.
A cheque can be neatly filled in, signed, and add up perfectly.
And still be drawn on an account that doesn't exist.
Only calling the bank tells you.
That's tier three.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: additionalProperties false, and stricter patterns everywhere.
Why?
These records are already well formed.
Wrong: more internal cross-field checks.
Why?
The records already agree with themselves.
Wrong: two independent instances, writing only matching records.
Why?
Both read the same delivery note, and agree.
Two contrasts to lock this in.
First.
A stricter schema versus a semantic check.
This is the single most common wrong move in the domain.
The team sees bad data.
Tightens the schema.
Sees no improvement.
Tightens again.
So ask yourself which one the stem describes.
If the value is well formed and wrong, the fix is a tier two or tier three check, in code.
If the value is malformed, the fix is enforcement.
Second.
Format failure versus absent data.
A format failure converges with specific feedback.
Absent data never converges.
So the loop needs two exits.
One.
Retry with feedback, for fixable errors.
Two.
An honest null, routed to a person, for information that isn't there.
We'll see similar routing of failure classes in the chapter on tool design and error handling.
There, errors are classed as transient, business, or permission.
And the words in a question that should switch this part on.
"Please try again," or "resends the same request."
That means the feedback lacks specifics.
"Pass rate went up but auditors found problems."
That means the feedback let the model overwrite evidence.
"The document never states it."
That means stop retrying, and allow null.
"Self-consistent but from the wrong document," or "a supplier we never used."
That means tier three.
That's part four.
If you remember one thing, make it this.
Check what the schema can't see, feed back the exact error including which side is right, cap the attempts, and never retry for data that isn't there.
Coming up in part five: designing efficient batch processing strategies.
